extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and executing point of view (first, second, third variants, omniscient, objective, unreliable narrators) in short stories, novellas, and novels, with practical examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose version of events is not to be trusted because of extraordinary limitations (e.g., autism, extreme youth, psychopathy, habitual lying) or deliberate deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reader understands early that ordinary skepticism does not apply; unreliable narration forces the writer to create two versions of the truth. If handled well the results can be intriguing and unsettling (example: Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart'). Exercise: write from the POV of an unreliable narrator who skews facts intentionally or unintentionally; make the reader understand the narrator's unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person single vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-person narrator with access to only one character's mind; the entire story is filtered through that point-of-view character's consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often combines advantages of first person (reader empathy) with an 'outside' voice that can craft language implausible for a first-person teller. Useful when the POV character lacks language/education to tell their own story (an outside narrator can better convey the character's shrewdness). Disadvantage: the point-of-view character must be present for everything that happens (limits what can be reported). Exercise: write a scene through the customer's eyes in a department-store clash, including thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view character (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The character whose point of view is being recognized by the author is the point-of-view character; this term applies across POV types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and consistently filter events through this character's consciousness when using single-vision POVs; recognition of whose thoughts and perceptions are being presented helps readers attribute opinions and descriptions correctly (example: Molly in 'Earth to Molly').

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person multiple vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-person narrator that alternates among two or more characters' perspectives to show events from different angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most often used in longer fiction (novellas, novels) because readers need space to learn multiple characters. Make distinct transitions between POV characters (don't switch mid-paragraph; use white space or chapter breaks). Use multiple POVs to emphasize differences and generate interest via disparities and juxtapositions; aim for good reason—don't switch if characters view the world identically. Trade-off: more flexibility/roominess and a collage-like view of the world, but you risk loss of focus and divided reader sympathy. Exercises: retell the same incident from salesperson, customer, bystander POVs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition conventions for POV switches
rubrics_metrics.description: When switching point-of-view characters, mark transitions clearly so the reader knows whose eyes witness events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not switch POV characters mid-paragraph. Use white space on the page or chapter breaks to mark transitions (Rick Bass example). Novelists often make switches at chapter breaks; sometimes alternate in a recognizable pattern so readers become less conscious of the switches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person omniscient (omniscience)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'all-knowing' narrator who can enter any character's mind, interpret events, describe incidents unobserved by characters, provide historical context, and reveal future events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omniscience gives freedom: enter minds, interpret, describe unobserved incidents, provide history, and reveal futures (exercise: demonstrate at least three of the five omniscient powers). Historically common (Fielding, Dickens, Tolstoy). Modern uses vary from subtle omniscience (Munro, Ondaatje) to conspicuous, self-aware omniscience (Kundera). Use omniscience to create suspense by supplying information unknown to characters (e.g., reveal an approaching disaster). Downsides: can call attention to the writer, seem impersonal, and be harder to manage; not for the faint of heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use omniscience for interpretation and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Omniscient narrator may interpret characters' reactions and draw conclusions, and provide historical/contextual background directly to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations should be gentle enough to leave room for reader inference (example: Welty). Omniscience can also be used self-referentially to comment on fiction itself (Kundera).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator has no access to any character's internal thoughts; all information must be revealed through action and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ultimate POV challenge—reveal background, characterization, conflict, and theme only through observable behavior and speech (journalistic, 'hard facts' approach). Strengths: sense of integrity and impartiality; prevents overexplaining. Downside: denies readers direct insight into characters' minds and emotions, potentially reducing immediacy and intimacy (Carver's 'Little Things' demonstrates credibility through reportage rather than explanation). Exercise: revise an omniscient wedding scene into objective POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second person
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator addresses 'you' and tells the reader what you did or said; can put the reader in the protagonist's place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second person can create intimacy and immediacy (McInerney's Bright Lights, Lorrie Moore's self-help voice), but risks feeling like a gimmick associated with certain authors. Use it inventively to make it fresh; otherwise proceed with caution. Exercise: rewrite a first-person passage into second person and compare effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional distance (camera distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceived closeness between narrator and characters, analogous to camera shots (long, medium, close-up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long shot: characters are distant; Medium shot: more detail; Close-up: narrator is close enough to feel sensations (e.g., 'felt the bitter cold air on his lips'). Emotional distance influences reader empathy; writers often pick a distance and stick with it, though it may change during a story for effect (Jane Smiley example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The temporal gap between when events occur and when the narrator tells them (present tense, recent past, long ago).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present tense narrows time distance and creates immediacy; past tense is conventional and often invisible to readers. Long time distance (events told as having occurred long ago) can produce nostalgia or suspicion due to memory erosion and reduce suspense since outcomes may be known; but it can offer valuable perspective (George Eliot example).

rubrics_metrics.name: POV contract with the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view establishes an implicit contract telling the reader what kind of story they are reading and what access to information they will have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking the POV contract (e.g., slipping into a minor character's head when using a limited POV) risks losing reader trust and the story's realism. Safeguards: write down rules about omniscience, reliability, and distance; check every paragraph against these rules during revision. If you must reveal another character's attitudes, show it through actions/dialogue rather than internal access. Deliberate, well-considered POV breaks can be effective, but casual lapses are harmful (student example with Ted's interiority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match POV to character abilities and authorial needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the POV that best serves the story's needs and the character's capacities (language ability, perception limits, need for irony or distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: third-person single vision is excellent if the POV character has limited verbal skills (the narrator 'stands behind the shoulder' to convey thoughts). If the narrator is a fictionalized self, using a third-person narrator can avoid self-indulgence. Consider what access and language are plausible for your chosen POV; use an 'outside' narrator to better convey a character's shrewdness when the character lacks eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify multiple viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple POV characters only when there's a clear reason—difference in viewpoint, community focus, or to create complex sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple viewpoints should reveal meaningful disparities or complementary perspectives (Tom Drury's community collage, Bass's juxtaposed characters). Avoid multiple POVs if characters perceive the world similarly, as the switch then serves no purpose.
